newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF says to come up with steps on DKB, Nomura soon.
newsitem.headline: MOF says to come up with steps on DKB, Nomura soon.

text.p: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) will come up with measures against Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) and Nomura Securities Co Ltd within a matter of days, Vice Finance Minister Takeshi Komura told a news conference on Monday.
DKB was fined 500,000 yen by Tokyo Summary Court on Monday for hiding loans to a racketeer.
It was accused of breaking the Banking Law, the first time a bank had been charged with such a violation.
Court officials said the court accepted prosecutors' recommendation on the size of the fine, the maximum allowed for violation of the Banking Law.
DKB and Nomura are both entangled in a high-profile scandal involving payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.

More than a dozen people, including top executives from the two financial firms, have been arrested in the affair, which coincides with the start of "Big Bang" reforms aimed at introducing more competition and global standards into Japan's long-sheltered financial sector.

The Finance Ministry filed a complaint last Friday with prosecutors against DKB and four former officials of the bank alleging that they had hidden information about problem loans to sokaiya Ryuichi Koike during a ministry inspection in October 1994.
The maximum penalty for such misreporting is only 500,000 yen, a fact which has led politicians to urge stiffer punishment to deter potential lawbreakers.
Also on Friday, prosecutors indicted former DKB chairman Tadashi Okuda for extending 11.78 billion yen in loans to Koike through an affiliated firm.

Payoffs to sokaiya, racketeers who buy shares in companies and try to extort money by threatening to expose dubious business practices or who are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings, have been illegal since 1983.
But many Japanese companies have found it difficult to cut off ties with the underworld.
